title: Why Some Conversations Don't Need a Script
author: Rod Naquin
summary: Rod Naquin traces his professional path from classroom 'talk moves' training to instructional coaching to explain why deliberate conversational techniques work equally well with fourteen-year-olds and adult colleagues — and why conversation feels easier than public speaking even without any such techniques at all. He grounds this in cognitive scientists Simon Garrod and Martin Pickering's research on 'interactive alignment,' the finding that the same mental system used to understand language is used to produce it, so conversation partners' word choices and sentence patterns automatically drift toward each other without either person deciding to make that happen. Naquin's key extension is that this alignment doesn't stop at vocabulary — it pulls along a shared 'situation model,' meaning people who converge on the same language end up converging on the same understanding of what's actually happening, essentially as a reflex rather than a strategy. Because natural alignment happens fastest under trust and slowest in guarded or evaluative relationships (a coach observing a teacher, for instance), Naquin argues deliberate talk moves matter most precisely in those harder rooms, offering a specific technique — the 'three-word echo,' repeating back the three or four highest-weight words from what someone just said, verbatim, followed by a pause — as a shortcut that speeds up alignment conversation is already built to do naturally.
points: The cognitive-science grounding (Garrod and Pickering's 'interactive alignment') explains a genuinely counterintuitive fact — conversation feels easier than a prepared speech despite requiring more real-time processing — because much of the coordination work happens automatically as a reflex, not a conscious strategy.

Naquin's key extension beyond vocabulary-matching is that alignment pulls along a shared 'situation model': when two people's language converges, their actual understanding of the situation converges too, almost as a side effect.

He identifies precisely where deliberate talk moves are most necessary — not natural, high-trust conversations, but guarded or evaluative ones (a coach observing a teacher) where natural alignment is slowed or blocked by role and history.

The 'three-word echo' technique is concrete and immediately testable: repeating a colleague's or student's own highest-weight words back verbatim (not a paraphrase) reliably prompts them to expand or self-correct, doing on purpose what conversation does automatically.
quotes: There's a small set of things a teacher can say — not content, just moves — that turn a flat discussion into a real one. Say more about that. Who can put that in their own words? Do you agree or disagree, and why?
They worked with adults almost exactly the way they worked with fourteen-year-olds, which surprised me more than it should have.

Conversation should be harder than giving a speech. You can't plan ahead, since you don't know what the other person will say. And yet none of this makes conversation feel hard. It's speeches that feel hard.
Multiply that across a whole conversation, and two people's language starts drifting toward each other without either one deciding to make that happen.
Two people who keep converging on the same language end up, almost as a side effect, converging on the same understanding of the situation.

Alignment happens fastest when trust is high and people are genuinely listening. It happens more slowly, or gets blocked, in rooms where people are guarded, where there's history, or where one person's job is technically to evaluate the other.
Not a paraphrase. Not "so what you're saying is." Just their exact words, echoed, followed by a pause or a follow-up question.
Most people, once they hear their own words handed back to them, will expand on the idea or correct it if you got it slightly wrong.
